originalTitle: How Gloria Steinem’s lifechanging stay in India shaped her approach to feminism
summary: The activist said her two years studying and travelling in country ‘made me who I am’
content: When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”. She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship. India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”. Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”. While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives. Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps. She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life. “At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote. Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis. She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.” India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India. When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris. Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters. She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”. At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”. But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road. On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”. Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later. Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves. But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957. Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk. She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”. In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards. “I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote. The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it. She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”. “If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.” Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement. “I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.” She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said. Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”. And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women. chineseTitle: 格洛丽亚·斯泰纳姆在印度改变生活的经历如何塑造了她对女权主义的态度
chineseSummary: 这位活动人士说，她在乡村学习和旅行的两年“造就了现在的我”
chineseContent: 1957 年，当格洛丽亚·斯泰纳姆 (Gloria Steinem) 的飞机降落在孟买时，她不可能知道她在印度的逗留会成为她后来所说的“关键的、决定人生的事件，使我成为今天的我”。她当时 22 岁，拥有史密斯学院的政府学位，并靠切斯特·鲍尔斯奖学金旅行。斯泰纳姆后来写道，印度“不仅是我一直想去的地方，而且还是一个逃离一个非常善良和诱人的男人的地方，我已与他订婚，并且知道我不应该结婚。”与来自纽约一个人脉广泛的家庭的飞行员布莱尔·乔齐诺夫结婚的前景让她感到非常沮丧，“因为婚姻对我来说意味着生命的终结”。资金短缺，所以她用一张免费机票换取了一篇“我至今仍感到内疚，因为我从未写过”的文章。在伦敦等待印度签证时，她发现自己怀孕了，并进行了非法堕胎——这一经历让她坚信，如果不控制生育，女性就无法控制自己的生活。斯泰纳姆本周去世，享年 92 岁，他带着对“永恒的美丽和珠宝大象”的浪漫期待抵达德里。他们很快就流离失所。从机场开车出来后，她“第一次看到亚洲的贫困”，看到人们睡在人行道和家门口。她住在德里大学领先的女子学院之一米兰达之家，沉浸在学生生活中。 “晚上在我们的房间里，我们进行长时间的会议，并被问到一切：基督徒对上帝的看法、西方内衣的复杂性、约会系统、美国奶牛产奶量，”斯泰纳姆写道。南卫理公会大学的拉什达·沙菲克 (Rashida Shafiq) 广泛记录了斯泰纳姆的印度岁月，她借鉴了她的同事的经验
